summary.text: The symmetric group on a set X is the group whose elements are the permutations of X, with function composition as the operation.
It is a group because composing permutations gives a permutation, the do-nothing bijection is the identity, and every permutation has an inverse.
Every permutation can be written as a product of transpositions, and the number needed is either always even or always odd.

facts.label: Transposition
facts.value: A permutation that swaps two elements and fixes the rest

facts.label: Parity
facts.value: A permutation needs either always an even or always an odd count of transpositions

facts.label: Alternating group
facts.value: The even permutations; for n ≥ 2 it has n!/2 elements

facts.label: Permutation groups
facts.value: Subgroups of symmetric groups carry this name

items.prompt: In the symmetric group on a set, which permutation acts as the identity?

options.label: The one that swaps every pair of elements
The one that reverses the whole order
The one that sends each element to itself
The one with the longest cycle

items.explain: The trivial bijection assigning each element to itself serves as the identity.

items.prompt: Why can any shuffle in the symmetric group be undone by another element of the same group?

options.label: Every bijection has an inverse function that is also a permutation
Every shuffle is its own opposite
Shuffles can be undone only when they are cycles
The identity can replace any shuffle

items.explain: A bijection has an inverse function that undoes its action, and that inverse is a permutation too.

items.prompt: One person writes a permutation as a product of three swaps. Could another person correctly write the same permutation as a product of four swaps?

options.label: Yes, any count of swaps can be used
Yes, if they add two extra swaps
Only if the set has an even size
No, the count is always odd or always even

items.explain: Representations are not unique, but the number of transpositions needed is either always even or always odd.

items.prompt: Two cycles in a permutation share no elements. Does the order in which you apply them matter?

options.label: No, disjoint cycles commute
Yes, it always changes the result
Yes, but only for cycles of length two
It matters only in small groups

items.explain: Disjoint cycles commute, so they can be applied in either order.

items.prompt: Student A writes a three-item cycle as (1 4 3) and student B writes (4 3 1). Are they describing different permutations?

options.label: Yes, the starting point changes the permutation
No, the same cycle can start at any point
Yes, unless the cycle has length two
No, but only when the cycles are disjoint

items.explain: A cycle can equally be written starting at a different point, so (1 4 3) and (4 3 1) name the same cycle.

items.prompt: Bubble sort only swaps neighbouring items yet can reach any ordering. Which fact explains this?

options.label: Disjoint cycles always commute
Every cycle has an order equal to its length
Every permutation is a product of adjacent transpositions
The even permutations form a normal subgroup

items.explain: Every permutation can be written as a product of adjacent transpositions, and bubble sort is an application of this fact.

paragraphs.heading: Every rearrangement
paragraphs.text: On any set, the symmetric group has as its elements every bijection of that set onto itself, and its operation is composing these functions. For a finite set, a permutation and a bijective function are the same thing: a rearrangement. The finite symmetric group Sₙ on n symbols holds every permutation of those symbols. There are n! such permutations, so Sₙ has order n!, its number of elements.

paragraphs.heading: Why it is a group
paragraphs.text: Checking that this is a group means checking closure, associativity, an identity and inverses. Composing two permutations of a set always gives another permutation of it. The bijection that sends every element to itself serves as the identity. Each bijection also has an inverse function that undoes it, and that inverse is a permutation too.

paragraphs.heading: Small cases
paragraphs.text: The symmetric group on n elements is abelian only when n is at most 2. On the empty set or a one-element set, where n is 0 or 1, the group is trivial, with just 1 element. The group Sₙ is solvable exactly when n ≤ 4.

paragraphs.heading: Where it shows up
paragraphs.text: The symmetric group matters in Galois theory, in invariant theory, in combinatorics and in the representation theory of Lie groups. In Galois theory, the symmetric group on n elements serves as the Galois group of the general degree-n polynomial. In invariant theory it acts on the variables of a function of several variables, and the functions it leaves unchanged are the symmetric functions. Cayley's theorem says that any group G is isomorphic to some subgroup of the symmetric group on G. Subgroups of symmetric groups are called permutation groups.

paragraphs.heading: Swaps and parity
paragraphs.text: A transposition is a permutation that swaps two elements and leaves all the others fixed, such as (1 3). Any permutation can be built as a product of transpositions. That way of writing it is not unique, but the number of transpositions needed is either always even or always odd. Permutations are called even or odd to match. The even permutations form the alternating group Aₙ, a normal subgroup of Sₙ with n!/2 elements for n ≥ 2.

paragraphs.heading: Neighbour swaps and sorting
paragraphs.text: Every permutation can even be written using only adjacent transpositions, swaps of the form (a a+1). This fact is what the sorting algorithm bubble sort puts to use. As with ordinary transpositions, such a product is not unique.

paragraphs.heading: Cycles
paragraphs.text: Take a permutation h that sends 1 to 4, 4 to 3 and 3 to 1, and leaves 2 and 5 alone. It is a cycle of length three, written (1 4 3), or equally (4 3 1) or (3 1 4). The order of a cycle equals its length, and cycles of length two are transpositions. Two cycles are disjoint when they move separate sets of elements, and disjoint cycles commute. For example, in S₆ the products (4 1 3)(2 5 6) and (2 5 6)(4 1 3) are equal.
